focus_areas: verification vs validation in ML systems
responsibility as a systems-engineering control loop paralleling MLOps
architectural propagation of specification failures
expanded correctness beyond latency and accuracy
rationale.question_strategy: Tier 2 minimal quiz with three questions that test the conceptual shift from reliability-only to responsibility-as-architecture. The MCQ grounds the verification/validation distinction in the Amazon scenario, the SHORT tests why continuous control-loop thinking matters, and the TF challenges the localized-bug intuition that traditional software engineering exports to ML.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Begin with the verification-versus-validation diagnosis on a concrete hiring scenario, move to explaining why the control-loop framing is mechanistically necessary, then synthesize with the architectural-propagation misconception traditional software would not encounter.
rationale.integration: Builds directly on the reader's existing MLOps control-loop vocabulary from @sec-ml-operations and the D·A·M taxonomy introduced in @sec-introduction, extending both to the responsibility context without redefining either.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 2 minimal quiz warranted: this section introduces the chapter's governing frame rather than a volume of standalone mechanics, and is followed by deeper application sections that carry most of the testable specifics.

questions.question: A hiring model meets its latency SLA, maintains 99.9 percent availability, and reports 87 percent aggregate accuracy, yet it systematically rejects qualified applicants whose resumes contain the word "women's." Applying the section's verification-versus-validation framing, which diagnosis best fits this outcome?
choices: The system failed verification because any unfair outcome is by definition a technical defect of the implementation.
The failure is primarily an operational reliability issue that responsible engineering practices address only after the serving pipeline becomes unstable.
The root cause is insufficient model capacity, so scaling up parameters would remove the disparity without changing the specification.
The system passed its stated technical checks but failed validation because those checks did not capture the responsible outcome the organization needed.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The model met its aggregate-performance and availability targets, so the stated technical checks passed, but those requirements omitted the organization's responsible hiring goal. The capacity-based answer makes the wrong diagnosis: a larger model would optimize the same flawed objective more faithfully, not less. The reliability-based answer conflates outage response with specification correctness, which is exactly the category error the section warns against.
questions.learning_objective: Classify a concrete ML deployment failure as verification-success-with-validation-failure and distinguish it from reliability or capacity issues.

questions.question: A team argues that a one-time ethics review before launch is sufficient because their model achieves strong aggregate accuracy and passes all latency checks. Using the section's MLOps analogy, explain why responsible engineering must instead be structured as a control loop, and give one specific measurement the one-time review would miss.
questions.answer: MLOps is the control loop for reliability because model performance degrades as data distributions drift; responsible engineering is the control loop for safety because outcome quality degrades as downstream populations and proxies drift, and both degradations are silent to the dashboards engineers already watch. A specific signal the one-time review misses is subgroup-level outcome disparity over time: a model reviewed at launch with 87 percent aggregate accuracy can develop a 30-point true-positive-rate gap for a minority subgroup months later without moving any latency or availability metric. The practical consequence is that responsibility requires the same ongoing measurement, feedback, and intervention infrastructure as latency SLOs, not a sign-off meeting that closes the loop.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the MLOps-to-responsibility control-loop parallel and identify a specific fairness measurement a one-time review cannot provide.

questions.question: True or False: Because machine learning systems are built from modular software components, a fairness defect originating in the training data can be isolated to a single module and fixed without architectural change, the way a null-pointer exception can be patched in one function.
questions.answer: False. ML data flows through shared representations, so a biased training signal can propagate across predictions rather than remain local. Unlike a null-pointer bug, the defect may be encoded in learned weights, so fixing it can require data-pipeline, objective, and evaluation changes across the D·A·M axes rather than a localized patch.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish localized software bugs from architecture-level ML failures and justify why specification-induced harm propagates across shared representations.

focus_areas: proxy variables reconstructing protected attributes
silent distribution-shift failures under green dashboards
alignment-gap mechanics and counterfactual evaluation
invariance vs slice-based vs boundary testing
architectural foreclosure of late-stage remediation
rationale.question_strategy: Tier 1 full quiz of five questions sampling the full arc: proxy-variable diagnosis (Amazon), silent distribution shift (sepsis model), alignment-gap reasoning (recommender), testing-method classification (invariance vs slice), and late-stage remediation (D·A·M architectural foreclosure). Replaces two flagged issues: the weak "more epochs" distractor in the proxy-variable MCQ and the trivia-fill for alignment gap.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Foundational proxy-variable diagnosis, then application of distribution-shift reasoning to a concrete clinical scenario, then mechanistic analysis of alignment-gap mitigation, then classification of testing methods, and finally a synthesis question on why late-stage remediation is structurally constrained.
rationale.integration: Builds on distribution shift and monitoring from @sec-ml-operations, the D·A·M taxonomy from @sec-introduction, and training-serving skew from @sec-ml-systems, extending each to the responsibility context without redefining them.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 1 full quiz warranted: this is the chapter's main technical section, introduces multiple silent-failure mechanisms, and develops the diagnostic framework readers must apply in later sections.

questions.question: Amazon's recruiting system penalized gendered terms and all-women's-college names without using an explicit gender label. Which diagnosis best explains why omitting the explicit attribute did not prevent harm?
choices: The fix was sound in principle; the system only needed additional bias-mitigation training epochs for the gender signal to fade from the learned weights.
Gendered terms, all-women's-college names, and correlated features acted as proxies for gender.
The problem was deployment-time distribution shift in the applicant pool rather than bias in the original training signal.
The problem was an optimization-objective mismatch that a different gradient-descent variant would have corrected during convergence.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Protected attributes can remain inferable from correlated features even when the explicit label is absent, so a model using gendered terms, college names, and other correlated features can preserve a discriminatory pattern without an explicit gender label. The deployment-drift answer misidentifies the failure mode: Amazon's harm arose in the training signal, not from an environmental shift after deployment. The optimizer-choice answer is a category error because changing the optimizer does not remove proxy information from the training data.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how proxy variables preserve discrimination after explicit protected-attribute removal and distinguish this failure mode from deployment-time drift.

questions.question: A hospital's sepsis prediction model continues to emit confident recommendations after an EHR update changes how vital signs are recorded, yet clinicians observe deteriorating outcomes for a subset of patients. All dashboards stay green. Walk through why this is a silent failure, identify two specific monitoring signals that would have caught it, and state the systems consequence for how teams instrument production ML.
questions.answer: The failure is silent because confidence scores, latency, and uptime can remain normal after an EHR change shifts the input distribution, so the model emits normal-looking predictions on changed inputs. Two signals could catch it: input-feature drift detection, using a task-calibrated statistic such as Jensen-Shannon divergence, could flag the EHR change, and disaggregated outcome monitoring against sepsis diagnoses could reveal subgroup degradation before aggregate metrics move. The systems consequence is that production responsibility monitoring must instrument the input pipeline and subgroup outcomes, not just confidence and latency, because health dashboards alone cannot see distribution-shift failures.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze a distribution-shift silent failure on a concrete clinical scenario and specify the monitoring signals that distinguish environmental failures from healthy operation.

questions.question: A recommendation team reports that engagement clicks rose 20 percent after deploying a new ranker, but month-over-month user satisfaction surveys dropped five percent and 30-day retention fell three percent. The team's director asks how to detect or prevent this class of failure before it recurs. Which engineering intervention best fits the section's alignment-gap framing?
choices: Hold out a random counterfactual slice of users at deployment, measure true-outcome metrics (satisfaction, retention) on that slice periodically, and trigger rollback when the proxy-true gap widens beyond a preset threshold.
Scale the model two-fold: a larger model will learn a richer representation of satisfaction and close the gap automatically.
Increase the weight of the clicks loss term: because the proxy correlates with the true goal initially, maximizing it harder will restore the lost correlation.
Retrain on more data: with enough examples, gradient descent will discover the satisfaction signal implicitly even when it is not in the training labels.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The section's alignment-gap analysis is a Goodhart-style decoupling between a measurable proxy (clicks) and a slower-to-measure goal (satisfaction); a counterfactual holdout with periodic surveys is one way to re-calibrate the proxy against the outcome. Scaling up the model or reweighting the clicks loss optimizes the proxy without adding satisfaction information. Retraining on more click-labeled data alone does not help because more examples cannot supply an outcome the loss function was never given.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the alignment-gap mechanism and select an intervention that re-anchors a proxy to a delayed true outcome.

questions.question: A lending team generates paired test applications that differ only in the applicant's first name ("John" vs "Jamal") while holding income, credit history, and debt constant, then compares approval probabilities. Which responsible-testing method from the section are they applying, and what failure mode does it surface?
choices: Boundary testing, which probes behavior at the edges of the input distribution where training data is sparse.
Slice-based evaluation, which partitions the test set into subgroups and reports per-slice aggregate accuracy.
Stakeholder red-teaming, which relies on affected community members to propose adversarial scenarios.
Invariance testing, which verifies that predictions remain stable when a feature the model should ignore is perturbed.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Invariance testing explicitly checks whether predictions change under a perturbation of an irrelevant attribute while holding task-relevant features fixed, which is precisely the counterfactual-pair construction the lending team is using. Slice-based evaluation answers a different question — per-subgroup aggregate metrics — and cannot isolate the causal effect of the name change. Boundary testing probes sparse regions of the input space, not counterfactual invariance. Red-teaming identifies scenarios to test but does not define the test construction itself.
questions.learning_objective: Classify responsible-testing methods by their construction and the specific failure mode each is designed to expose.

questions.question: True or False: Once a model's architecture, loss function, demographic-attribute collection, and monitoring pipeline have been fixed, a later ethics-board review can still implement equally effective fairness interventions as engineers could have at design time.
questions.answer: False. The section shows that early architectural decisions can narrow remediation options downstream: adding fairness constraints may require retraining, post-hoc explanations may be inadequate for some accountability needs, and a data pipeline that omits demographic attributes can prevent direct disaggregated evaluation. By review time, the board may face substantial data, model, or pipeline changes rather than an equally effective patch, which is why responsibility requirements belong in design reviews.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why late-stage review cannot substitute for engineering-time responsibility decisions, grounded in the D·A·M architectural-foreclosure mechanism.

focus_areas: 100$\times$ data requirement for minority subgroup evaluation
model cards as deployment guard rails vs historical records
fairness-metric diagnosis from confusion-matrix statistics
price-of-fairness quantification and Pareto-frontier decisions
EU AI Act and GDPR Article 22 architectural obligations
rationale.question_strategy: Tier 1 full quiz of five questions sampled across the section's subsections: predeployment representation statistics, model-card guard-rail function, fairness-metric diagnosis from confusion matrices, price-of-fairness reasoning (replacing the editorial ORDER flagged by the audit), and regulatory explainability obligations.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with representation arithmetic, move through documentation function and fairness-metric diagnosis, then quantitative fairness-accuracy trade-off reasoning, and close with regulatory-architecture synthesis.
rationale.integration: Extends monitoring and rollback vocabulary from @sec-ml-operations, confusion-matrix concepts from @sec-ml-workflow, and quantization/compression cost analysis from @sec-model-compression into fairness, documentation, explainability, and regulatory-compliance territory specific to this chapter.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 1 full quiz warranted: this section operationalizes the chapter's principles into concrete engineering workflows and carries the densest set of quantitative anchors (100$\times$ multiplier, TPR disparities, 15M EUR penalties).

questions.question: A team wants 10,000 face images from a subgroup that makes up 1 percent of users, enough in this example to estimate one binomial performance rate to roughly ±1 percentage point at 95 percent confidence. What total collection should random sampling yield in expectation?
choices: About 100,000 total images, because confidence intervals shrink roughly linearly with the combined dataset size regardless of subgroup prevalence.
About 10,000 total images, because the target test-set size is already fixed and subgroup composition is handled automatically by the model's training procedure.
About 1,000,000 total images in expectation, because a 1 percent subgroup supplies about one of every 100 randomly sampled images.
Sample-size reasoning applies only to training data; evaluation confidence scales with the number of gradient-update steps, not with the subgroup sample count.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Dividing the target 10,000 subgroup samples by the 0.01 prevalence yields an expected 1,000,000 total samples—the 100-fold multiplier the section derives. The realized subgroup count is random, so this is an expectation rather than a guarantee; if random collection is impractical, stratified collection can target the subgroup directly. A 100,000-image collection would yield only about 1,000 subgroup images in expectation. The confidence statement concerns estimating one binomial rate, not automatically detecting a one-point gap between two rates.
questions.learning_objective: Apply subgroup prevalence to derive an expected collection size and interpret the associated confidence assumption.

questions.question: A team argues they will write their model card after launch so it can accurately reflect observed behavior. Explain why the section calls this a guard-rail failure, and describe one specific scope-creep scenario that a predeployment model card would have blocked but a post-launch card would not.
questions.answer: A model card written before deployment specifies intended use, excluded use cases, and validated populations, but it becomes an enforcement artifact only when downstream deployment gates check those fields before repurposing the model. Written after launch, the card becomes a historical summary that cannot prevent scope creep already underway. For example, a vision model marked "not validated for high-stakes screening" can be blocked from a security workflow when a gate enforces that exclusion, whereas a card written six months into the deployment would merely document the use after exposure began. The systems consequence is that only an up-front card paired with enforcement can constrain gradual expansion.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why model-card timing determines whether it functions as a deployment constraint or a retrospective record, and identify a concrete scope-creep scenario this timing controls.

questions.question: In the loan-approval worked example, Group A (majority) has a true positive rate of 90 percent and Group B (minority) has a true positive rate of 60 percent, while both groups share the same false positive rate of 20 percent. Evaluating each fairness criterion against these numbers, which statement is correct?
choices: Demographic parity is satisfied because the false positive rates match across groups.
Equalized odds is satisfied because one of its two component rates matches across groups.

Equal opportunity is violated by the 30-point true-positive-rate gap, and equalized odds is also violated because equalized odds requires both true-positive-rate and false-positive-rate equality, so matching false positive rates alone is not sufficient.
Only calibration is implicated, because true-positive-rate disparities affect model accuracy rather than fairness.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Equal opportunity requires equal true-positive rates among qualified applicants, so a 30-point gap violates it directly — qualified minority applicants face a 30-point higher rejection rate than equally qualified majority applicants. Equalized odds requires both true-positive-rate and false-positive-rate equality, and the shared false-positive rate cannot rescue the criterion when the true-positive-rate component is violated. Demographic parity is about equal approval rates, not equal error rates, so matching false-positive rates is not its criterion. The calibration-only framing misreads the problem: true-positive-rate disparities are fairness violations regardless of their aggregate-accuracy effect.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose equal-opportunity and equalized-odds violations directly from confusion-matrix statistics and distinguish them from demographic parity and calibration.

questions.question: Stakeholders ask a hiring team to close a 20-percentage-point true-positive-rate gap between two groups by lowering the decision threshold for the disadvantaged group. Using the Pareto-frontier framing and the price-of-fairness calculation from the section, analyze what the team should present to stakeholders and why threshold adjustment alone is a design choice, not a technical fix.
questions.answer: Under the section's assumptions, closing the 20-point TPR gap adds $4,000 of successful-hire value but $6,000 of false-positive cost per disadvantaged-group applicant, a net $2,000 loss. That is 20 percent of that group's $10,000 baseline utility; an aggregate percentage is underdetermined without the other group's baseline utility. The team should present the Pareto frontier and these assumptions to stakeholders because threshold adjustment chooses a trade-off rather than eliminating it.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify the price-of-fairness trade-off for a concrete threshold-adjustment scenario and justify why Pareto-frontier presentation is the correct engineering deliverable to stakeholders.

questions.question: A European lender plans solely automated credit decisions with significant effects. Assuming the system is high-risk under the EU AI Act and no Article 6(3) exception applies, which architectural consequence follows most directly?
choices: Because deeper models are more accurate, explainability engineering can be deferred until after legal approval closes.
Aggregate fairness metrics alone are sufficient because individual applicant explanations are irrelevant in financial decisions.
EU regulation applies primarily to foundation models, so a loan classifier with fewer than a billion parameters can be deployed without explainability infrastructure.
The architecture must support risk management, logging, human oversight, meaningful information about automated logic, and applicable rights to human intervention and contest.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Under the stated assumptions, EU AI Act duties include risk management, logging, transparency, and human oversight. GDPR Article 22 applies to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, subject to its exceptions and safeguards; Articles 13–15 add information duties. Aggregate fairness metrics do not discharge applicable individual information, intervention, or contest rights. The size-based framing misreads the legal structure: covered use and decision context, not model parameter count alone, determine the obligations.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how high-stakes regulatory obligations translate into specific architectural capabilities that must be engineered in at system inception rather than retrofitted.

focus_areas: efficiency as a three-channel responsibility obligation (carbon, cost, accessibility)
edge-deployment power and latency fit for model selection
inference-dominated TCO reasoning and 40:1 inference-to-training ratio
carbon intensity vs algorithmic efficiency comparison
rationale.question_strategy: Tier 1 full quiz of five questions covering efficiency philosophy (with a stronger distractor addressing the unified responsibility claim, per the audit flag), edge deployment-fit reasoning, quantitative TCO analysis (replacing the flagged trivia FILL with a SHORT that applies TCO to a concrete optimization decision), inference-vs-training leverage, and carbon-region vs algorithmic-improvement comparison.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with the conceptual link between efficiency and responsibility, move into a deployment-fit decision with specific power and latency budgets, then analyze TCO as an engineering lever, and close with a carbon-vs-algorithm trade-off comparison.
rationale.integration: Synthesizes quantization and model-compression numbers from @sec-model-compression, hardware-acceleration energy efficiency from @sec-hardware-acceleration, and inference-serving economics from @sec-model-serving into responsibility-oriented cost and carbon accounting.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 1 full quiz warranted: this section introduces a cross-cutting engineering argument with deployment constraints, a scenario-specific inference-training ratio, and carbon accounting that shape deployment decisions.

questions.question: A team can deploy either a full-precision model or a quantized version that preserves task accuracy while cutting inference compute by roughly 4$\times$. According to the section, why does this efficiency choice count as a responsibility decision rather than purely a performance decision?
choices: When the compute reduction lowers measured service demand, quantization can reduce energy and cost and may enable deployment on cheaper hardware.
Quantization is primarily a responsibility tool because it automatically reduces fairness disparities by making all user groups equally cheap to serve.

Quantization is a pure performance optimization that should be evaluated separately from responsibility, because fairness, carbon, and cost belong to distinct engineering layers with different owners.
Quantization matters mainly for training-time energy: production inference is usually a minor fraction of lifecycle resource use, so the responsibility payoff is small.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The section's efficiency-as-responsibility argument is that reducing measured service demand can pay out across several channels: lower energy and carbon when the deployment uses less electricity, lower serving cost when pricing reflects the reduced demand, and access to cheaper hardware when the optimized model fits it. The reductions are not automatically 4$\times$ because utilization, memory traffic, batching, grid intensity, and pricing also matter. The fairness answer conflates efficiency with disparity reduction, and the training-dominance answer treats a scenario-specific TCO ratio as universal.
questions.learning_objective: Justify why efficiency interventions serve environmental, economic, and accessibility responsibilities simultaneously rather than being a separable performance concern.

questions.question: A wearable device has a 500 mW sustained power budget and a 500 ms end-to-end inference latency requirement. Using the section's deployment-comparison data (TinyML at roughly 50 mW / 200 ms, MobileNetV2 at roughly 1.2 W / 40 ms, EfficientNet-B0 at roughly 1.8 W, ResNet-50 much larger), which model selection is the correct responsible-engineering choice, and why?
choices: ResNet-50, because larger models achieve better energy efficiency per accuracy point once their throughput is amortized through batching.

TinyML model, because its 50 mW power draw fits 10$\times$ under the budget and its 200 ms latency fits under the 500 ms requirement, so it is the only option that satisfies both constraints simultaneously.
MobileNetV2, because 1.2 W is close enough to the 500 mW target that the gap is operationally negligible on modern battery-management hardware.
EfficientNet-B0, because its smartphone-grade footprint guarantees it also fits wearable constraints once the form factor is reduced.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Only the TinyML model satisfies both the 500 mW power ceiling (at 50 mW, a 10$\times$ margin) and the 500 ms latency ceiling (at 200 ms); every other option exceeds the stated power budget by at least 2$\times$. MobileNetV2 draws 2.4$\times$ the stated 500 mW budget, so "close enough" is quantitatively wrong. The smartphone-to-wearable extrapolation is the common mistake the section warns against: wearable budgets are materially tighter than smartphone budgets. Batching arguments do not rescue ResNet-50 on a device that serves one query at a time.
questions.learning_objective: Apply edge-deployment power and latency constraints to select a model architecture that satisfies both budgets and reject the smartphone-to-wearable extrapolation.

questions.question: Using the section's illustrative three-year TCO breakdown (training ~2 percent, inference ~73 percent, operations ~25 percent), compare a 50 percent reduction in training time with a 20 percent reduction in dedicated per-query accelerator service demand. Which has higher leverage, and by roughly what dollar-savings ratio?
questions.answer: Under the scenario's unbatched, non-overlapped service-demand assumptions, the inference reduction has higher leverage: 20 percent of the inference term saves about 14.7 percent of total cost, while 50 percent of the training term saves about 0.9 percent, a ratio near 16-to-1. Batching, concurrency, and realized utilization would change the TCO shares, so the conclusion must be recomputed for a real deployment.
questions.learning_objective: Compare two optimization proposals using TCO framing to quantify dollar-cost leverage in an illustrative inference-dominated scenario.

questions.question: True or False: For an identical model and serving workload, migrating deployment from a carbon-intensive cloud region to one powered by abundant renewable energy can reduce inference emissions more than a one-time modest algorithmic efficiency improvement.
questions.answer: True under the stated comparison: emissions equal energy use times grid carbon intensity, so a sufficiently lower-carbon region can outweigh a modest energy reduction. The result depends on measured energy and regional carbon intensity; no universal reduction factor applies.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate how grid-carbon-intensity infrastructure choices can outweigh algorithmic efficiency gains in overall emissions for the same workload.

questions.question: Training GPT-3 consumed roughly 1,287 MWh of electricity. At the scenario's carbon intensity of roughly 0.429 kg CO~2~ per kWh, which combined approach reduces the footprint of future foundation-model training runs?
choices: Reducing model size to under one billion parameters, accepting the corresponding accuracy loss, because parameter count is the only significant driver of training energy.
Deferring all training until grid carbon intensity reaches zero, since any non-zero intensity produces emissions that cannot be justified ethically.
Switching the entire training pipeline from FP32 to FP16 without other changes, because numerical precision alone accounts for the bulk of training energy use.
Measure and reduce training energy through model and system optimization, then reduce emissions further through carbon-aware scheduling and lower-carbon regions.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Training emissions combine measured energy use with grid carbon intensity, so two levers can stack: model and system optimization can reduce the energy required for the workload, while carbon-aware scheduling or region selection can reduce emissions per unit of electricity. Parameter count and numerical precision are possible levers, not sole drivers, and their effects must be measured for the actual workload. The zero-carbon answer is not an engineering intervention, and the FP16-only answer overstates one factor.
questions.learning_objective: Identify complementary infrastructure-layer responsibility levers for large-scale training emissions and reject single-lever framings.

right-to-erasure requires automated lineage across derived artifacts
privacy-by-design architecture for always-listening systems
security / privacy / audit role distinctions (replacing flagged ORDER)
GDPR Article 17 financial penalties driving system requirements
rationale.question_strategy: Tier 1 full quiz of five questions spanning the governance domains. Replaces the flagged ORDER (which imposed a strict dependency among security, privacy, and audit that the section does not support) with a SHORT that distinguishes their operational roles. Covers enforcement-vs-policy framing, lineage requirements, privacy-by-design architecture, and regulatory penalty magnitude.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with the governance-as-infrastructure framing, move through an erasure-scenario lineage analysis, then a privacy-by-design architectural choice, then role differentiation among security, privacy, and audit, and close with a quantitative regulatory-risk claim.
rationale.integration: Extends data-governance, lineage, feature-store, and privacy vocabulary from @sec-data-engineering and monitoring infrastructure from @sec-ml-operations into explicit compliance architecture for production ML.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 1 full quiz warranted: this section introduces concrete infrastructure obligations and translates legal requirements into architectural constraints.

questions.question: In 2023 Meta received 390M EUR in fines over the legal basis, transparency, and fairness of behavioral-advertising processing, not a data breach. Which diagnosis best captures the chapter's governance lesson?
choices: Governance replaces the need for model monitoring once regulators sign off on the data pipeline, because certification transfers ongoing responsibility to the certifier.

Policy claims become demonstrable only when access controls, privacy mechanisms, lineage tracking, and audit logs make each requirement technically enforceable across the data lifecycle — otherwise compliance is an assertion rather than evidence.
Governance is primarily about publishing external-facing datasheets and model cards so that readers outside the organization can assess the system.
Governance applies only to raw storage, since derived features, model artifacts, and deployment workflows are downstream and fall outside the data lifecycle.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The decision shows that governance includes a lawful basis, fair processing, and clear disclosure, not merely data security. Technical controls and records can make those obligations demonstrable across the data lifecycle by preserving access, transformation, and model-lineage evidence where applicable. Certification does not transfer ongoing compliance. The datasheet-only answer confuses documentation with enforcement, and the raw-storage-only answer is too narrow because governance extends through features, models, and deployment workflows.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why data governance must be implemented through enforceable technical infrastructure and distinguish this framing from documentation-only or raw-storage-only views.

questions.question: A European user of a voice-assistant service invokes GDPR Article 17 right-to-erasure. Explain why a manual search across storage systems can be unreliable and too slow to satisfy the request, and describe what automated infrastructure the compliance architecture should provide.
questions.answer: A distributed pipeline can fan a source record into features, embeddings, checkpoints, caches, and deployed versions, so a manual search is unreliable. Automated lineage should identify candidate downstream artifacts and route each through the applicable workflow: deletion, invalidation, access restriction, unlearning or retraining, or legal review. Audit records are not categorically deleted or retained; their treatment depends on purpose, minimization, retention duties, and governing law.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why distributed ML pipelines make manual deletion difficult and identify the lineage-and-automation infrastructure that supports right-to-erasure compliance.

questions.question: The Lighthouse KWS system is an always-listening keyword-spotting voice assistant deployed in users' homes. Which architectural combination best reflects the section's privacy-by-design approach for this deployment, and why?
choices: Stream all ambient audio to a cloud service that applies strong centralized privacy controls after collection, since centralized processing allows more sophisticated mechanisms than any edge device can run.
Retain raw audio indefinitely on secure cloud storage, because the future retraining value of long-horizon voice data outweighs privacy concerns when access is properly encrypted.

Run wake-word detection on-device, transmit only necessary post-detection audio or privacy-protected updates, and enforce retention and deletion policies on any retained audio, minimizing personal-data exposure.
Rely on role-based access control as the sole privacy mechanism, since privacy concerns reduce to limiting who can query the data and RBAC solves exactly that problem.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. The section's privacy-by-design architecture combines three complementary moves: on-device detection (ambient audio need not leave before detection), purpose limitation (only necessary post-detection audio or privacy-protected updates cross the network), and retention limits (any retained audio has a bounded lifetime), so the attack surface is reduced by design rather than only by policy. Centralized cloud collection inverts the principle by maximizing the data exposed before protection, so a breach or insider access exposes more. Indefinite retention treats future training value as a blank check, which the section rejects. RBAC-only misreads the threat model: RBAC limits who can query data, while privacy also limits what authorized actors can learn about individuals, which is a separate problem addressed by techniques such as differential privacy and data minimization.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the privacy-by-design architectural pattern for always-listening systems and distinguish privacy minimization from access-control mechanisms.

questions.question: A teammate argues that security, privacy, and audit are essentially the same concern because each restricts data access. Using the section's governance stack, distinguish the operational role of each and give one concrete failure mode that would not be caught if the other two were fully implemented but that mechanism were missing.
questions.answer: Security answers who can reach the data at all: access controls, authentication, and encryption define the perimeter within which all other mechanisms operate. Privacy answers what information authorized actors can learn about individuals: differential privacy, minimization, and aggregation limit inference even when access is legitimate. Audit answers who actually did what: logs of access and transformation events create the accountability trail that makes the other two verifiable under scrutiny. A system with strong security and privacy but no audit cannot respond to a regulatory subpoena that asks which employee accessed which records on which date — the access happened legitimately, the data was appropriately anonymized, but the organization cannot prove either claim and fails the audit. Symmetrically, strong security plus audit without privacy still leaks individual-level information to every authorized data scientist, and strong privacy plus audit without security lets unauthorized actors bypass the whole stack. The mechanisms are complementary accountability layers, not redundant restrictions.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the operational roles of security, privacy, and audit mechanisms in the governance stack and identify a concrete failure mode specific to each missing mechanism.

questions.question: True or False: An ML team can reasonably defer lineage infrastructure until its first GDPR deletion request because source records can then be found manually.
questions.answer: False. A source record can propagate into features, checkpoints, caches, and deployed artifacts. Building lineage only after a request arrives may leave the team unable to identify affected artifacts or complete the applicable workflow on time. Penalty categories and amounts depend on the specific infringement.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why up-front lineage infrastructure is a prerequisite rather than an optional engineering investment.

focus_areas: aggregate-metric concealment of subgroup disparity
proxy-variable reconstruction of protected attributes
training-only environmental accounting misses the dominant term
documentation without enforcement fails under scope creep
rationale.question_strategy: Tier 2 minimal quiz of four questions testing whether readers can recognize the chapter's recurring mistaken mental models and connect them to quantitative evidence. Adds one question (documentation-scope-creep TF) to the original three to strengthen coverage of the pitfall section's full arc while staying within the Tier 2 range.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with aggregate-metric misreading on a concrete loan scenario, move to proxy-variable reasoning about attribute-removal remediation, then tackle documentation-enforcement misconception, and close with the inference-dominated environmental-accounting synthesis.
rationale.integration: Consolidates lessons from the responsibility-gap, checklist, efficiency, and governance sections into warning heuristics anchored in the chapter's TPR disparities and scenario-specific inference-to-training ratio.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 2 minimal quiz warranted: this section recaps prior arguments through anti-patterns rather than introducing new mechanics, but the misconceptions are high-value synthesis checks.

questions.question: A deployed loan-approval model reports 85 percent aggregate accuracy, but disaggregated evaluation shows qualified applicants from one demographic group have a true-positive rate 30 percentage points lower than another group. Which pitfall from the section does this outcome most directly illustrate?
choices: The mistaken belief that fairness can be assessed from aggregate metrics alone, because strong overall accuracy masks the subgroup disparity that only disaggregated evaluation surfaces.
The mistaken belief that documentation automatically enforces deployment constraints, so a written model card prevents misuse even when no technical control blocks it.
The mistaken belief that removing sensitive attributes from training data always eliminates bias, so explicit-attribute exclusion guarantees proxy-free predictions.
The mistaken belief that training costs dominate lifecycle cost, which leads teams to over-optimize training at the expense of inference.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The 30-percentage-point true-positive-rate gap under 85 percent aggregate accuracy is the canonical flaw-of-averages failure: the aggregate is a weighted average that hides the minority-group disparity, which only disaggregated evaluation reveals. The documentation-enforcement answer describes a different pitfall about deployment scope creep, not aggregate-metric concealment. The attribute-removal answer is also real but refers to why fairness persists after explicit-attribute removal, which is the next fallacy in the section and does not explain the metric mechanic here. The training-cost answer addresses environmental accounting, not fairness metric reporting.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the aggregate-metric pitfall when strong overall performance conceals substantial subgroup disparity and distinguish it from other fallacies in the section.

questions.question: A team proposes removing race and gender features from their model, then deploying without further fairness evaluation because "the model cannot discriminate on attributes it does not see." Drawing on the Amazon recruiting and Optum healthcare-cost cases from the chapter, explain why this reasoning creates false confidence rather than eliminating bias, and identify the specific engineering work still required.
questions.answer: Protected attributes can remain inferable through correlated proxies that carry demographic signal: Amazon's reported examples included gendered terms and all-women's-college names despite no explicit gender label, and the Optum system encoded unequal access through healthcare-cost history because cost was an imperfect proxy for need; correcting the bias increased the share of Black patients identified for additional help from 17.7 percent to 46.5 percent. The engineering work still required includes causal and proxy analysis, validated fairness interventions such as constrained optimization where appropriate, per-group outcome monitoring in production, and the disaggregated evaluation this chapter develops. Attribute removal alone is insufficient, and teams that stop there can deploy a model that discriminates while appearing compliant.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why proxy variables undermine naive attribute-removal approaches and specify the causal-analysis, fairness-constraint, and monitoring work required for actual bias mitigation.

questions.question: True or False: Because a well-written model card explicitly states intended use and excluded use cases, teams that publish comprehensive model cards can treat deployment-scope compliance as handled without additional technical controls.
questions.answer: False. This is the documentation-as-accountability pitfall: a model card specifying "not validated for high-stakes decisions" has no enforcement power when a system is repurposed without access-control or deployment-gate restrictions. Documentation provides transparency but requires paired operational controls—monitoring dashboards, subgroup-disparity alerts, and deployment gates tied to intended use—to function as enforcement.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why documentation without enforcement fails under scope creep and identify the operational controls that must pair with model cards.

questions.question: True or False: For a production ML system, reporting only training-run carbon accurately characterizes its long-term environmental burden.
questions.answer: False. Training-only reporting omits serving emissions. In the chapter's illustrative high-traffic, unbatched service-demand scenario, inference-to-training cost is about 40:1; other systems may have different ratios, so lifecycle accounting must measure both terms rather than assume either dominates.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why training-only environmental accounting is misleading for production ML systems and quantify the inference-dominance ratio that drives the misclassification.

translation of ethical concerns into measurable engineering invariants
dual-purpose nature of prior optimization techniques (performance and responsibility)
iron-law and D·A·M frameworks extended to wider objective set
rationale.question_strategy: Tier 2 minimal quiz of three questions that check whether the reader integrated the chapter's central thesis and can connect responsibility tools to the book's broader ML-systems framework. Rewrites the "second master" MCQ's weaker distractors per the audit flag to preserve partial truth and force sharper discrimination.

rationale.integration: Explicitly connects this chapter back to the iron law from @sec-introduction, quantization and pruning from @sec-model-compression, hardware acceleration from @sec-hardware-acceleration, monitoring from @sec-ml-operations, and governance from @sec-data-engineering.

questions.question: After reading the chapter, which statement best captures the summary's claim about how responsible engineering relates to traditional systems engineering?
choices: Responsible engineering is ML systems engineering done completely: a system that ignores fairness, efficiency, transparency, or governance is technically incomplete, not merely ethically imperfect.
Responsible engineering is primarily a legal and ethical overlay that engineering teams apply after the technical system is feature-complete.
Responsible engineering is a specialty concern that matters only for high-risk regulated domains such as healthcare and criminal justice.
Responsible engineering replaces performance optimization with ethical review, so teams adopting it trade throughput and latency for fairness and transparency.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The chapter's closing thesis is that correctness in ML must extend beyond latency and accuracy to encompass fairness, efficiency, transparency, and governance as measurable properties of a complete system, applied from inception. The legal-overlay answer inverts the chapter's argument: the Amazon and COMPAS cases show that late-stage review may not repair architecturally constrained problems. The specialty-domain answer is contradicted by the efficiency and TCO material, which applies to every production system regardless of regulatory classification. The replacement framing misreads the chapter: earlier optimization techniques (quantization, pruning, hardware acceleration) serve both masters simultaneously rather than being traded off.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the summary's thesis that responsibility is engineering completeness and distinguish it from overlay, specialty-domain, and replacement framings.

questions.question: The summary argues that responsibility concerns become tractable only when translated into measurable engineering invariants. Explain what this means by contrasting a vague principle with a specific invariant, and describe how the invariant integrates into an existing monitoring workflow.
questions.answer: A vague principle such as "be fair" gives engineers nothing to implement, test, or monitor, whereas an invariant such as "per-group true-positive-rate disparity <5 percentage points, measured hourly, with an alert if exceeded for 15 minutes" is a concrete target that slots directly into existing SLO infrastructure. The fairness dashboard can sit next to the p99-latency dashboard, with shared alerting and on-call workflows. Remediation may trigger investigation or, where labels arrive quickly and rollback is safe, an automated rollback. Responsibility becomes actionable and auditable only at this level of specification; at the principle level, claims cannot be verified and interventions cannot be triggered.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how concrete measurable invariants make responsibility concerns actionable by integrating into existing SLO and monitoring workflows.

questions.question: The summary argues that earlier optimization techniques taught in the book serve a "second master" beyond performance. Which pairing most precisely reflects that dual-purpose claim?
choices: Monitoring primarily detects latency regressions, so fairness monitoring requires entirely separate infrastructure that does not share code paths with reliability monitoring.

Hardware acceleration improves throughput and energy efficiency at the chip level, but grid-scale carbon impact depends purely on regulatory-policy decisions that engineers cannot influence through technical choices.

Quantization, pruning, and monitoring can improve throughput and latency while potentially reducing carbon per query, broadening deployment to lower-cost hardware, and surfacing silent subgroup disparities — the same techniques can serve performance and responsibility through shared mechanisms.

Quantization yields sustainability benefits (lower energy per inference) but those benefits are independent of accessibility, since cheaper hardware deployment is a product-management concern rather than a consequence of compute reduction.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. The chapter's synthesis is that shared mechanisms can pay out across dimensions: fewer bytes and operations can reduce measured energy and hardware requirements, while subgroup monitoring can extend the existing observability stack. The monitoring-as-separate-infrastructure answer misses that integration. The sustainability-separated-from-accessibility answer overlooks that lower compute can broaden feasible deployment, although the effect is workload-dependent. The policy-only carbon answer is also incomplete because grid carbon intensity multiplies measured energy rather than replacing efficiency as an engineering concern.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how prior optimization and monitoring techniques serve both performance and responsibility objectives through shared mechanisms rather than through separable work.
